rv.q: It’s a richly colourful and assured recreation, and a brave, unquestionable triumph for the Old Vic.
The overwhelming impression, though, is that this is feast of show.
It’s possessed of a surging emotional swoop and visual audacity that bursts its way into your heart.
Max Webster’s production has tableaux to ravish the eye and enough quirks to keep the clock ticking along so the evening’s three-and-a-half hours (or more) seldom seem to lag.

This play has much going for it... But it is far too uneven.

However conscientious the stage version, it can’t match Bergman’s genius for using the camera to pick up revealing detail, such as the moment when Alexander instinctively recoils as his dying father grips his hand with ferocious tightness.
Yet this version by Stephen Beresford never quite convincingly makes the case for the transition from screen to stage.
Why it cries out for this format isn’t fully answered.
Despite its length, the play never drags under director Max Webster, carrying us along with its alluring combination of drama, comedy and a touch of magic.
The result is engrossing and rewarding.
This lush, haunting bedtime story unfolds in the sumptuous Old Vic as if it was written for it.
If, in the end, it doesn't entirely succeed, it's also neither dull nor merely dutiful.
Many elaborately described onstage meals later (don’t go to this play hungry), you emerge at the end of “Fanny and Alexander” having been riveted, but rarely enriched.

You may want to catch this production for the performances of matriarch, daughter-in-law and grandson (though I can't vouch for the three other Alexanders, nor which you might see when); or you may do better simply to sit down with the full five-hour version of a film that repays constant re-viewing.
There are some banal and even boring scenes which prevent the production from achieving greatness. But beautiful performances compensate for the occasional lacklustre sequences.

cn.t: Bergman's epic receives a mixed-to-positive reception, with critics praising strong performances (especially Wilton) and its theatrical ambition, but questioning whether the 3.5-hour adaptation captures the film's emotional intensity and nightmare vision.
